name: Non-surgical rhinoplasty (liquid nose job)

lead: Non-surgical rhinoplasty, or a liquid nose job, uses injectable filler to reshape the nose without cutting. Practitioners use it to fill depressions, camouflage a dorsal hump, raise the tip angle or add projection, giving a straighter, better-projected profile that is visible immediately.

A filler, most commonly hyaluronic acid gel, is placed in selected points to change contour by adding volume and creating optical straightening. It can only add volume and does not reduce nose size. The literature is mostly retrospective series and reviews, including a case series of 511 procedures over 16 years.

paras: It is a short clinic treatment with little or no recovery, appealing to people who want a change without surgery. Results from hyaluronic acid fillers are temporary, and the enzyme hyaluronidase can dissolve them.

The nose's vessels connect with the ophthalmic artery, so accidental intravascular injection can cause skin ischaemia and, rarely, vision loss. Other reported effects include swelling, bruising, asymmetry and granulomas. Regulatory approval of fillers varies by product and use.

angle.text: Filler is injected to smooth a bridge bump, lift the tip or add projection without surgery, with the change visible immediately. Results are temporary, and it is seen as a reversible, lower-commitment alternative to surgical rhinoplasty.

lead: Non-surgical rhinoplasty, also called liquid rhinoplasty or a liquid nose job, is a cosmetic procedure that reshapes the nose with injectable filler instead of surgery.[1] It is used to smooth a bump on the bridge, fill dents or asymmetries, lift a drooping tip or add projection, with results visible straight away and no incisions.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes it as using fillers such as collagen or hyaluronic acid to fill depressed areas, lift the angle of the tip or smooth bumps on the bridge, without changing the size of the nose.[1] Most of the plastic-surgery literature concerns hyaluronic acid, which lasts for a limited time and can be dissolved with the enzyme hyaluronidase.[3][4] Reviews report patient satisfaction above 90 percent in prospective studies, and a 2023 systematic review described it as a quick option for minor shape concerns, while case reports document rare but serious vascular complications including skin necrosis and vision loss.[5][6][3][7][8]

In looksmaxxing culture it is classed with hardmaxxing procedures as a reversible, lower-commitment alternative to surgical rhinoplasty, and as a way to preview the effect of a straighter profile before committing to surgery.
infobox: Mostly hyaluronic acid fillers; others have been used[1][20]
Smooth hump, lift tip, add projection or fill depressions[1]
Temporary; reviews of hyaluronic acid fillers report roughly 8 to 12 months for several authors, with longer durations in others[4]
Hyaluronic acid can be dissolved with hyaluronidase[3]
Vascular occlusion with skin necrosis or vision loss[3][18][8]
The nose is not an FDA-approved filler area; the agency lists it among areas where it recommends against injecting[18]
Above 90% average in a systematic review of 11 studies[7]

paras: The procedure is performed in a clinic with a needle or cannula to place small amounts of filler at defined points along the nose, such as the dorsum, radix and tip.[6][9] Published methods include a five-point technique, a deep columellar approach, and a 'five-principle, five-step' method.[6][9][10] Wikipedia notes that the technique is limited to adding volume and cannot reduce nasal size.[1] Practitioners describe an 'optical' effect in which adding volume at the root or tip makes the bridge look straighter or a hump look smaller, rather than removing it.[1][11]

A narrative review describes the nonsurgical category as including dermal fillers, thread lifting and botulinum toxin injections, and lists the qualities of an ideal filler as safe, painless to inject, hypoallergenic, long lasting and giving consistent, natural-feeling results.[11] A randomised trial has also tested a non-surgical nose-shaping device, the Nasella Nose Former, in patients with and without prior surgery.[12]

sections.h: How it is used to change appearance
paras: Users and clinicians describe several goals: camouflaging a dorsal hump, raising a low or drooping tip, adding height to a flat bridge, evening out dents or irregularities after trauma or earlier surgery, and balancing the profile to the chin and forehead.[1][6][13] A 2025 systematic review of non-surgical rhinoplasty after prior surgical rhinoplasty (20 articles, 2,048 patients) found hyaluronic acid used in 67 percent of patients, a high degree of satisfaction, and a low rate of major complications, and described the technique as useful for correcting subtle to moderate defects left after surgery.[13]

Because the effect appears in minutes with little downtime, proponents also discuss it as a way to try out a new profile before deciding on surgical rhinoplasty. A review of dorsal augmentation graft options notes that graft-based surgery has its own complication risks, which is the context in which filler is considered as an alternative.[14]

Early attempts at nasal soft-tissue augmentation used paraffin wax and silicone, which Wikipedia describes as biologically harmful, and physicians shifted to minimally invasive techniques with modern fillers after about 2000.[1] The surgical operation itself has a long history, from reconstruction described in ancient Indian and Egyptian texts to the first modern endonasal rhinoplasty in 1887, and 2020-2021 saw before-and-after nose-job videos spread on TikTok under the #NoseJobCheck tag.[1]

Reviews in the early 2020s describe the filler approach as increasingly popular, and papers from 2020 to 2025 propose standardised injection protocols, including a five-point technique (2022), a deep columellar approach tested in a case series of 511 procedures over 16 years (2022), and a five-principle, five-step method (2023).[5][6][9][10]

Hyaluronic acid is the most commonly used filler in published series.[15][13] Wikipedia's page on hyaluronic acid describes it as a naturally occurring sugar that is used in fillers and that can be broken down by hyaluronidase.[16] Thread lifting and botulinum toxin injections are also grouped under the non-surgical label in reviews.[11]

Forum posts show that some users discuss using products other than hyaluronic acid. In one looksmax.org thread a user describes having a nasal dent filled with a silicone product, and a reply notes that filler at the nose tip can complicate a later rhinoplasty.[17] The FDA states that injectable silicone for aesthetic purposes can cause long-term pain, infection, scarring, embolism, stroke and death.[18]

A retrospective single-centre analysis of a five-point technique assessed safety and effectiveness for insufficient projection and other indications in adult patients.[6] A 2021 systematic review of hyaluronic acid nasal filler searched from 2005 to 2021, included 11 prospective or experimental studies, and found average patient satisfaction above 90 percent.[7] A 2023 systematic review of 16 studies concluded that the technique appears to be a quick and safe option for minor nose shape problems, particularly with hyaluronic acid, while calling for further discussion and research.[2]

A 2023 literature review on longevity found that, of 16 selected studies, six authors reported durations of 8 to 12 months and the others reported results lasting longer than that.[4] Wikipedia's hyaluronic acid page gives a general range of about 6 to 12 months for such fillers.[16]

A review of safety in nasal filler use and a study of the ultrasound anatomy of the dorsal nasal artery address how vessel location relates to risk.[5][15] The nose's blood supply communicates with the ophthalmic artery via branches of the facial artery, so accidental injection into a vessel can cause skin ischaemia and, rarely, partial or complete vision loss.[3]

A 2019 case report in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery described reversal of post-filler vision loss and skin ischaemia with high-dose pulsed hyaluronidase injections.[3] A European Journal of Ophthalmology case describes a 29-year-old woman who presented with sudden visual loss, ptosis and ophthalmoplegia after non-surgical rhinoplasty in a beauty salon in West London.[8] Wikipedia's hyaluronic acid page lists erythema, itching, pain, bruising, vascular occlusion and granulomatous reactions among filler complications.[16]

The US Food and Drug Administration lists approved uses of absorbable fillers such as wrinkles, lip, cheek, chin and hand augmentation, and does not list the nose; its page names the glabella, nose and periorbital area among places where it recommends against injection.[18] The FDA calls unintended injection into a blood vessel the most concerning risk, which it says is uncommon but can cause tissue death, vision abnormalities including blindness, and stroke, and it advises seeking immediate care for unusual pain, vision change or skin turning white, grey or blue near the injection site.[18]

Published evidence consists mainly of retrospective series, technique descriptions, anatomical studies and complication case reports, with a small number of prospective studies. A retrospective analysis of a five-point technique reported safety and effectiveness outcomes,[6] and a case series of 511 procedures over 16 years described a deep columellar approach.[9] Systematic reviews in 2021, 2023 and 2025 summarised satisfaction and complications,[2][7][13] a 2025 systematic review covers hyaluronic acid injection techniques and complications,[19] and reviews of nonsurgical and liquid rhinoplasty summarise techniques.[20][21] The complication literature includes a case report of vision-loss reversal with hyaluronidase.[3]

The procedure is categorised among hardmaxxing options that people consider as a trial run for surgical rhinoplasty or as an alternative to it. On looksmax.org a poster described booking a non-surgical rhinoplasty to fill a dent in the bridge and to consider hiding a minor dorsal hump, calling it part of his plan to 'ascend', while a reply noted that fillers at the tip can cause problems if rhinoplasty is considered later.[17]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the procedure is discussed as a lower-commitment nose fix and a preview of surgery.[17]

claims.claim: A liquid nose job gives an instant straighter profile with no recovery.
The results last only a limited time and can be dissolved.
It can make the nose smaller.
It is risk-free compared with surgery.
Nose filler can complicate a later surgical rhinoplasty.
Non-hyaluronic or permanent fillers give longer-lasting nose results.

timeline.event: First modern endonasal (closed) surgical rhinoplasty is performed, according to Wikipedia's history of the operation.[1]
After about 2000, physicians shift from paraffin and silicone to modern fillers for nasal augmentation, according to Wikipedia.[1]
Prospective randomised trial of a non-surgical nose-shaping device published.[12]
Case report of reversing post-filler vision loss and skin ischaemia with high-dose hyaluronidase.[3]
Review of safety in nasal filler use; #NoseJobCheck videos begin spreading on TikTok.[1][5]
Systematic review of hyaluronic acid nasal filler reports average satisfaction above 90 percent.[7]
Five-point technique analysis and 511-procedure deep columellar case series published; ultrasound study of the dorsal nasal artery.[6][15][9]
Reviews of nonsurgical rhinoplasty, longevity and the five-principle, five-step method appear.[20][10][2][4]
Systematic review of non-surgical rhinoplasty after prior rhinoplasty (2,048 patients) reports low major complication rates.[13]
